title: Kidney replacement that is portable and affordable at global scale

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a complete kidney-replacement service that people can use at home or in resource-constrained settings, with adequate removal of excess fluid and waste solutes and substantially lower demands for water, power, consumables, specialist staff and infrastructure. Portability is one requirement; the larger goal is dependable, affordable treatment that local services can sustain at population scale. This defines the target capability, rather than an achievement established by the supplied evidence.

Wearable dialysis with regenerated dialysate provides one technical route. A sorbent-based system recirculates a small dialysate volume through materials that remove waste, while battery-powered pumping supports treatment away from stationary equipment. The supplied human study demonstrates elements of this approach. Completing the concept also requires safe treatment access, infection prevention, reliable alarms, usable controls, maintenance, repairs and dependable supplies. The service need not be implanted or reproduce every biological kidney function.

significance.text: If safe and inexpensive treatment could operate without a specialized dialysis center or large supplies of purified water, it could reduce location and infrastructure barriers to life-sustaining kidney replacement. The revolutionary consequence would be expanded access and greater freedom over where treatment occurs. Demonstrated wearable fluid and solute removal provides a technical basis for this possibility, but the supplied trial does not establish expanded access, affordability or improved population outcomes.

As a conditional service-level synthesis, successful deployment could make treatment feasible in more communities and reduce dependence on repeated travel to centralized facilities. These benefits would still depend on financing, safe access care, patient and caregiver support, maintenance and reliable supply chains. Moving equipment into the home can redistribute work and costs rather than eliminate them, so portability alone is insufficient evidence of affordability or global scalability.

The analogy to a biological kidney has important limits. This concept targets practical replacement of enough fluid and solute regulation to sustain patients; it does not require restoration of all kidney functions or independence from other medical care. Its impact should therefore be judged by clinical outcomes, treatment burden and access, rather than by resemblance to an intact organ.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central engineering challenge is sustained, reliable fluid and solute control in a compact system suitable for independent use. In the supplied wearable trial, excessive carbon dioxide bubbles in the dialysate circuit and variable blood and dialysate flows contributed to stopping the study. These findings identify concrete barriers in gas management, pumping and circuit reliability. Sorbent regeneration and miniaturization must work together without compromising controlled treatment delivery.

Safe operation outside intensive supervision remains a distinct challenge. The study identified a need for longer outpatient and home studies, including assessment during walking and operation by patients. Reliable alarms, understandable controls, safe access and infection prevention must support treatment under everyday conditions. Short supervised operation cannot establish the long-term safety of continuous treatment or the ability of patients and caregivers to manage it independently.

For the proposed global service, the additional unresolved capability is maintaining clinical performance while reducing total resource requirements and cost. Consumables, staffing, repairs, training and supply continuity must remain manageable in the intended settings. These are proposed engineering and service requirements, not findings of the 2016 trial. The supplied evidence does not establish whether the complete capability remains unavailable as of November 2026.

current_state.text: Gura and colleagues’ study, published in JCI Insight on June 2, 2016, evaluated a wearable sorbent-based artificial kidney in seven participants. Five completed the planned 24 hours of treatment. The trial stopped after the seventh participant because of device-related technical problems, including excessive carbon dioxide bubbles in the dialysate circuit and variable blood and dialysate flows. The result demonstrates short-term wearable treatment functions while exposing reliability problems; it does not demonstrate a completed replacement service.

The system used sorbent regeneration and battery-powered pumping, with an approximate blood-circuit volume of 65 mL and dialysate-circuit volume of 375 mL. Observed fluid and solute removal and the small regenerated dialysate circuit support the technical feasibility of compact treatment. Circuit volume, however, is not a measurement of total treatment water consumption and cannot establish water savings or affordability across the whole service.

The trial involved intensive inpatient monitoring, and participants received conventional dialysis before exposure to the wearable device. Its short duration and treatment context limit conclusions about sustained standalone performance. The authors explicitly identified long-term safety as unestablished and called for longer outpatient and home studies. The study did not establish long-term independent home use, total treatment costs or population-scale delivery.

The supplied research mentions a reported 2026 dialysate-free rabbit prototype, but provides no inspectable source or search entry supporting that report. Its findings and publication status therefore remain unverified here. The claimed earlier publisher-access failure is also not documented in the supplied evidence. These limitations do not show that the prototype report is false, and they do not weaken the documented 2016 results. The empty freshness search record leaves the broader field’s status as of November 2026 unassessed.

According to the supplied review, the evidence assessment covered the full main article in retained HTML and a 15-page PDF, rather than only its abstract. Linked supplements and figure images were not inspected. The quantitative details retained here were supported by article prose, so they do not require interpretation of those uninspected materials.

completion_criteria.text: A proposed convincing clinical demonstration would establish sustained safety and effectiveness during outpatient and independent home use, with outcomes competitive with an appropriate available dialysis comparator. It should measure fluid and solute control, clinically consequential complications, treatment interruptions and the ability of patients and caregivers to operate the system. Longer home evaluation follows directly from limitations identified in the supplied trial; the final study design would need prespecified follow-up duration, endpoints and comparator margins.
completion_criteria.label: Sustained outpatient and home outcomes competitive with appropriate dialysis

completion_criteria.text: For the affordability and scale objective, proposed demonstrations should include diverse settings, including low-resource services, and independent audits of total treatment costs and resource use. Accounting should cover equipment, consumables, water, power, access care, staffing, training, maintenance, repairs and patient or caregiver work. Local teams should demonstrate dependable procurement, fault response and continued treatment delivery. These are proposed criteria for this concept, not established consensus standards or conclusions of the wearable trial.
completion_criteria.label: Audited costs and resource use across dependable low-resource services

completion_criteria.text: Independent replication across sites and operators should establish how performance varies with patient needs and service conditions. Evaluations should report eligibility restrictions, required backup care, failure modes and settings where the service cannot operate safely or economically. Reliability and affordability thresholds must be specified before evaluation. Successful finite studies would establish demonstrated breadth within those boundaries, rather than literal suitability for every patient or health system.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replication defines limits against prespecified reliability and affordability thresholds

related_concepts.text: Based on the supplied roster, NEP-04, “A durable, implantable artificial kidney,” is the closest overlap: both pursue artificial replacement of kidney functions. NEP-04 makes durable implantation central, whereas NEP-05 makes portability, affordability and scalable service delivery central and can use an external device. An implantable approach could contribute to NEP-05 if it met its access and cost requirements, but neither concept’s completion would automatically establish the other.

NEP-01, regrowing functional nephrons, and NEP-02, reversing established fibrosis, aim to restore function within existing kidneys. NEP-03, manufacturing transplantable human kidneys, and NEP-06, supplying durable animal-donor kidneys, pursue biological replacement organs. NEP-07 addresses donor-specific immune tolerance in kidney recipients. These concepts overlap with NEP-05 in their ultimate treatment goals, while pursuing different biological capabilities and delivery requirements.

NEP-08, a durable root-cause treatment for ADPKD; NEP-09, durable reversal of diabetic kidney disease; and NEP-10, broad prevention of severe acute kidney injury, target disease treatment or injury prevention. Success could reduce the need for kidney replacement among affected patients. NEP-05 instead addresses provision of replacement therapy when it is needed. These distinctions follow from the supplied roster titles; they do not establish the detailed scope or progress of those entries.

change_log.reason: These supported details distinguish demonstrated short-term operation from sustained independent treatment.

change_log.reason: Small circuit volumes support compact-system feasibility but do not quantify whole-service resource savings.

change_log.change: Retained the reported 2026 rabbit prototype as an unverified report and qualified the claimed inspection history.
change_log.reason: No supplied source or search entry verifies either assertion; missing evidence does not establish falsity.

change_log.change: Expanded proposed completion demonstrations to include comparative outcomes, independent replication, full cost accounting and operational boundaries.
change_log.reason: The clinical and global-access objectives require separate evidence, with thresholds specified prospectively.

unresolved_issues: The complete capability’s availability and the broader field’s status as of November 2026 remain unassessed by the supplied freshness record.
The identity, findings and publication status of the reported 2026 dialysate-free rabbit prototype, and the claimed prior publisher-access failure, remain unverified.
Long-term clinical performance, independent home reliability, whole-service water and power requirements, affordability and scalable delivery are not established by the supplied trial.
Proposed evaluations still require follow-up duration, clinical endpoints, comparator margins, cost boundaries and reliability thresholds; no numerical resolutions are supplied.

Related-concept distinctions are limited to the supplied roster titles. The review’s recommendation to remove the NEP-04 comparison was not adopted because that title now supports a bounded comparison, without establishing NEP-04’s detailed scope.

brief.title: Portable kidney care people can afford worldwide
possible: People whose kidneys have failed could receive dependable, affordable treatment at home or in communities with limited resources. A portable system would remove excess fluid and waste from their blood while needing much less water, power, equipment and specialist support.
why: This could bring life-sustaining treatment to communities that cannot support a specialist treatment center. Patients could spend less time traveling for care and have more freedom over where treatment happens.

sources.who: Victor Gura, Matthew B. Rivara and colleagues
sources.showed: A wearable device removed excess fluid and waste during a closely supervised hospital trial involving seven people. Gas bubbles and unstable flows caused technical problems that stopped the trial.
sources.cited_for: The trial demonstrated short-term wearable treatment and exposed reliability problems.
sources.not_established: It did not establish sustained independent home treatment, affordability or dependable delivery at scale.

sources.showed: A preliminary conference report described assisted treatment in centers for 29 participants. Blood chemistry stayed generally stable, with no serious adverse device effects (SADEs), meaning serious harm caused by the device.
sources.quote: No SADEs or device deficiencies with potential to cause a serious adverse event occurred.
sources.cited_for: Repeated treatment with a portable system showed encouraging short-term safety under staff supervision.
sources.not_established: The preliminary study had no comparison group and did not establish independent home use, long-term safety or affordability.

sources.showed: A conference report described a trial involving three patients. A portable system removed waste comparably to conventional dialysis, a treatment that filters blood, during brief sessions.
sources.quote:
All patients tolerated and completed treatment with Neokidney
TM
with no adverse events.
sources.cited_for: The small trial supported the feasibility of portable treatment that recycles its cleaning fluid.
sources.not_established: Participants also received conventional treatment, so the trial did not establish sustained treatment with the portable device alone.

shown: Gura and colleagues demonstrated that a wearable device could remove fluid and waste in a closely monitored trial involving seven people. Technical problems stopped the study.

Bolhuis and colleagues reported repeated assisted treatment with the portable Neokidney system in 29 participants. This preliminary conference report extends experience beyond a brief demonstration, but treatment still took place in centers with staff assistance.
missing: Long-term independent home treatment has yet to demonstrate safety and effectiveness comparable to appropriate available dialysis.
Compact systems still need dependable pumps, gas control, alarms and safe connections to patients, with protection against infection.
Affordable services still need to demonstrate lower total resource use, reliable supplies, local repairs and manageable work for patients and caregivers.

milestones.label: Sustained home treatment with competitive health outcomes
milestones.explanation: Trials would have to show sustained safety and effectiveness in outpatient and independent home use, comparable to appropriate dialysis. This would establish that patients and caregivers can manage dependable treatment.

milestones.label: Audited affordability and dependable care in low-resource settings
milestones.explanation: Independent audits across diverse services, including low-resource settings, would have to measure all costs and resources alongside dependable delivery. This would establish whether local teams can sustain affordable care.

milestones.label: Independent replication establishes where treatment works
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to repeat results across sites and operators against reliability and affordability thresholds set beforehand. This would define which patients and settings the service can safely support.

uncertain: The necessary follow-up length and acceptable differences from existing treatment remain to be defined.
Cost boundaries and thresholds for reliability and affordability remain to be agreed before evaluation.
It remains unclear how performance and costs would change across patient needs and local service conditions.

page.title: Portable dialysis below US$5 per day
page.definition: A system that can travel with the patient would remove waste and excess fluid through an external blood filter (hemodialysis) or the lining of the abdomen (peritoneal dialysis). It would cost less than US$1,000 to manufacture at scale and less than US$5 a day to run, operate on solar power, purify water from any source and match the safety and effectiveness of existing dialysis. In a home pilot of the prize-winning design, patients prepared peritoneal dialysis fluid from tap water. The pilot tested the fluid without using it for treatment.

goal.need: In 2010, at least 2.284 million people may have died prematurely because they could not get dialysis or a kidney transplant. For someone using four 2-litre bags a day for peritoneal dialysis, about three tonnes of fluid must be delivered each year. A cheaper machine leaves that freight bill in place. Preparing fluid locally could reduce the cost of home treatment. Solar power and local water could also bring dialysis within reach of remote communities, where patients still need access to clinical care.

figures.caption: Worldwide provision and estimated need for kidney replacement in 2010
figures.note: Kidney replacement includes dialysis and transplantation. These estimates describe 2010.

statements.body: International Society of Nephrology, Asian Pacific Society of Nephrology and The George Institute for Global Health, Affordable Dialysis Prize
statements.quote: It needed to cost less than US$1000 to build at scale and provide treatment for less than $5 a day
statements.context: The International Society of Nephrology restated the 2015 prize objectives in 2018.

completion.title: A portable dialysis system meets the Affordable Dialysis Prize's cost, power, water and clinical targets.
completion.criterion: A functioning portable dialysis system meets the published prize targets together: manufacturing cost below US$1,000 at scale; treatment running cost below US$5/day; operation on solar power using any water source; and safety and effectiveness equal to existing dialysis systems. Portability follows KHI terminology: transportability that permits treatment beyond the home and clinic.
completion.set_by: International Society of Nephrology, Asian Pacific Society of Nephrology and The George Institute for Global Health, Affordable Dialysis Prize established in 2015; objectives restated by ISN in 2018. Portability terminology: Kidney Health Initiative.
completion.threshold_quote: It needed to cost less than US$1000 to build at scale and provide treatment for less than $5 a day, be able to run on solar power, using any water source, yet be as safe and effective as existing dialysis systems.
completion.basis: The prize sponsors set design targets and awarded the prize in March 2016 while the prototype was in development. In the subsequent home pilot, three patients filled 60 peritoneal dialysis bags using potable Sydney tap water in homes with reliable electricity. Two bags had detectable endotoxin. No participant received dialysis with the prepared fluid. Comparative clinical performance and operation under the full prize conditions remain unverified.

milestones.title: A dialysis prototype passes functional and safety testing for its intended operating environment.
milestones.criterion: Functional testing verifies that the prototype performs as designed. A system-level hazard analysis and evidence of electrical safety and electromagnetic compatibility address the intended environment, including hazards specific to home use when that use is claimed.
milestones.set_by: FDA, Hemodialysis Delivery Systems guidance, section VIII; this recommendation was written for hemodialysis. The Liberty PDx clearance documents the corresponding performance-testing stage for peritoneal dialysis.
milestones.threshold_quote: functional testing that demonstrates that the device performs as designed and expected;

milestones.title: A dialysis system delivers treatment in people with initial safety and device function assessed.
milestones.criterion: An early human feasibility study documents delivery of dialysis with the investigational system and assesses device function and initial clinical safety.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 2013 guidance on early feasibility medical-device studies; this development stage applies across device types.
milestones.threshold_quote: Early feasibility studies allow for early clinical evaluation of devices to provide proof of principle and initial clinical safety data.

milestones.title: Patients or care partners deliver prescribed dialysis at home in a clinical investigation.
milestones.criterion: After training, patients or care partners deliver prescribed dialysis at home. For nocturnal home hemodialysis, compare adverse events, delivery of the prescribed dose and completion of scheduled treatments with in-clinic use. For wearable peritoneal dialysis, the AWAK protocol trains patients for independent use, sets an individual prescription and measures the proportion of treatments completed over seven days at home. Its study defined completion as delivering at least 70% of the prescribed sorbent dialysis in a treatment.
milestones.set_by: FDA nocturnal home hemodialysis guidance, section 5, for the clinic comparison. AWAK Technologies protocol NCT05827588 for the seven-day peritoneal dialysis assessment, with the per-treatment endpoint specified in the Kidney Week abstract.
milestones.threshold_quote: use the AWAK PD system at home for at least 7 days

milestones.title: A dialysis system receives FDA clearance with home treatment included in its indications.
milestones.criterion: FDA issues a 510(k) decision letter finding the dialysis system substantially equivalent to a legally marketed device, and the indications for use accompanying the decision explicitly include home treatment.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 510(k) substantial-equivalence process and the home-use indications enclosed with individual clearance decisions.
milestones.threshold_quote: This order “clears” the device for commercial distribution

milestones.title: A purifier produces water that meets the quality limits for preparing the intended dialysis fluid.
milestones.criterion: Test treated water from a specified feedwater source. For fresh hemodialysis fluid, the water meets ISO 23500-3 chemical limits, has fewer than 100 colony-forming units/mL and contains less than 0.25 endotoxin units/mL. For point-of-care peritoneal dialysis, apply the water specification for that system. The AMIA protocol tests water before the sterilizing filters against ISO 13959 and requires no bacterial growth and less than 0.03 endotoxin units/mL in the holding bag after filtration.
milestones.set_by: ISO 23500-3:2024, sections 4.1–4.3, for hemodialysis water. The registered AMIA protocol BXU011787 specifies the sampling points and limits for its peritoneal dialysis system.
milestones.threshold_quote: The quality of the dialysis water, as specified in 4.2 and 4.3, shall be verified upon installation of a water treatment system.

not_found: No published demonstration was located that combines the prize's cost limits, solar operation, source-water capability and comparative clinical performance in one functioning system.
The prize documents located do not define clinical comparison margins, follow-up duration, complete treatment-cost boundaries or inflation adjustments.
No externally set population-coverage threshold for worldwide delivery was located in the prize, KidneyX or KHI materials.
The AWAK publisher page supplied the abstract but restricted access to the full article.
No statement from a nephrology society or prize body disputing the value or feasibility of the combined targets was located.

results.finding: In 7 inpatients using the wearable artificial kidney, achieved ultrafiltration differed from prescription by a mean of 3 ± 15 mL.
results.detail: Excess carbon dioxide exceeded the device's degassing capacity, and tubing kinks and variable pump function contributed to fluctuating blood and dialysate flows.
results.quote: Ultrafiltration was accomplished as intended, with a mean difference between prescribed and achieved ultrafiltration over the study period of 3 ± 15 ml.

results.finding: Five of 7 inpatients completed the planned 24-hour hemodialysis treatment with the wearable artificial kidney.
results.detail: The trial stopped after the seventh participant because of cumulative device problems, including excess carbon dioxide bubbles and variable blood and dialysate flows.
results.quote: Of 7 enrolled subjects, 5 completed the planned 24 hours of study treatment.

results.finding: In 29 participants, Neokidney correctly detected the sole episode of sorbent exhaustion.
results.detail: The episode arose during assisted in-center treatment and provides evidence about the exhaustion-detection function.
results.quote: Sorbent exhaustion occurred only once, at the end of a session in which estimated urea removal exceeded the system's specified maximum urea-removal capacity. This was correctly detected by the device and there was no occurrence of hyperammonemia in any of the 474 sessions.

results.finding: Among 29 adults treated with Neokidney, zero serious adverse device effects were reported.
results.detail: The abstract identifies spKt/V as the primary efficacy endpoint and leaves the observed estimate and confidence interval unreported.
results.quote: As of August 31st, 2026, 29 participants were included and completed 474 Neokidney sessions (95% of planned Phase 1&2 sessions). No SADEs or device deficiencies with potential to cause a serious adverse event occurred.

results.finding: In 3 patients, NeoKidney maintained regenerated dialysate bicarbonate within ±4.7% of the spent dialysate concentration.
results.detail: The functional result comes from the investigational treatment sessions. I classified the supplied source as an ASN conference-program abstract.
results.quote: The dialysate bicarbonate concentration was maintained within ±4.7% of the concentration in spent dialysate.

results.finding: All 3 patients completed NeoKidney hemodialysis with zero adverse events.
results.detail: Each patient received one investigational session, followed by conventional dialysis to complete their usual treatment time.
results.quote:
A total of 3 patients were recruited. All patients tolerated and completed treatment with Neokidney
TM
with no adverse events.

results.finding: SC+ Machine simulated-home validation reported zero critical use errors that could lead to a hazard. Sample size unreported.
results.detail: Participants received training or completed self-training. The summary names the bench tests and says the supporting documentation was submitted.
results.quote:
participants are able to safely and effectively use the SC+ Machine without making critical 
errors that could lead to a hazard.

results.finding: SC+ delivered hemodialysis in the HOME RUN pivotal study (n=32), with mean standardized weekly Kt/V of at least 2.8 throughout the home phase.
results.quote:
Results of the HOME RUN Study demonstrate SC+ Machine safely and effectively delivers 
treatment to subjects in both an in-clinic and in-home setting.

results.finding: HOME RUN participants (n=32) delivered SC+ hemodialysis at home, with mean standardized weekly Kt/V of at least 2.8 in every home phase.
results.detail: The 75% cutoff defined the evaluable population. The excerpt supplies no phase-by-phase comparison of scheduled-treatment completion.
results.quote:
The 
study demonstrated that the mean weekly standardized Kt/V was consistently above the 
target of 2.1 during all weeks of the in-clinic phase (≥2.3 in all phases C1-C8) and all 
weeks of the in-home phase (≥2.8 in all phases H1-H8).

results.quote:

results.finding: In 60 patients, Quanta SC+ had a median absolute fluid-removal deviation of 0.06 kg/h.
results.detail: The paper also reports that SC+ met fluid-removal limits in controlled laboratory verification. The cable failure ended one treatment early and one circuit of blood was lost, with no reported symptoms.
results.quote: Median deviation (positive or negative) from idealized fluid removal was 0.06 kg/h (25th and 75th percentiles, 0.03 and 0.09, respectively).

results.finding: Quanta SC+ delivered 1,333 evaluable hemodialysis treatments in 60 patients.
results.detail: Patients switched to SC+ without substantive prescription changes. The results section and Table 1 identify 60 qualified patients, and Table 1 lists 63 enrolled.
results.quote: 60 patients were enrolled in the study, resulting in 1,333 evaluable treatments.

results.detail: One participant withdrew after a vascular access thrombosis considered possibly device-related.
results.quote: 5.2 events per 100 treatments during the in-home phase (5.2%; 95% CI, 3.29-7.11).

results.finding: Quanta home hemodialysis in 34 evaluable adults achieved a mean weekly standardized Kt/V of 3.0.

results.finding: Among 19 adults who completed the Carry Life UF crossover study, mean ultrafiltration increased by 381 mL versus control.
results.quote: The UF volume primary outcome was met as Carry Life UF was superior to control in a prespecified superiority margin of 250 ml, mean increase 381 ml, 95% confidence interval (CI, 285 to 477).

results.finding: In the Carry Life UF crossover study, 19 adults completed the study, with device treatment prescribed three days per week at home.
results.quote: During the Carry Life UF arm, one daily 2.5% dextrose exchange was replaced with a Carry Life UF treatment 3 days/wk (1.5% dextrose solution for PD fill, 11 or 15 g/h glucose dose) and a 1.5% dextrose exchange 4 days/wk.

results.finding: NxStage reports that System One Plus passed bench verification and validation. The number of test units is unstated.
results.detail: The manufacturer reports an overall pass. The summary does not give results by standard or describe the system-level hazard analysis.
results.quote:
Verification and validation was conducted to characterize the proposed device and the 
predetermined acceptance criteria were met.

results.finding: FDA cleared one device, the NxStage System One Plus, for home hemodialysis under K170469.
results.detail: The indications require a physician’s prescription and a trained, qualified operator.
results.quote: The System is also indicated for home hemodialysis, including home nocturnal hemodialysis.

results.finding: Lilliput APD passed simulated-treatment functional verification and underwent IEC 60601-1:2005 electrical safety testing. Sample size unspecified.
results.detail: The testing results come from the sponsor’s 510(k) summary. The FDA decision establishes substantial equivalence.
results.quote: Electrical Safety testing was performed in accordance with IEC 60601-1:2005.

results.finding: FDA cleared one system, Lilliput APD, under K212522 for adult chronic peritoneal dialysis in home and clinical settings.
results.detail: The supplied text gives the home indication in section 5.6 of the 510(k) summary. Page 3, the enclosure page, contains only the submission number in the supplied extraction.
results.quote:
The Lilliput™ APD System is indicated for adult chronic peritoneal dialysis in home and 
clinical settings
.

results.finding: Tablo, 30 enrollees: 94% of evaluable home treatments met the prescribed ultrafiltration tolerance.
results.quote: In the ITT cohort, 94% of the treatments in‐center and 94% of the treatments in‐home successfully achieved the goal.

results.finding: Tablo delivered 1,806 hemodialysis sessions across the two observation periods in a trial with 30 enrollees.
results.quote: There were 1806 treatments conducted during the 2 observation periods of the study.

results.finding: Tablo home hemodialysis participants (n=28) completed 99% of scheduled treatments.
results.quote: Eight hundred eighty‐four hemodialysis sessions were completed during the In‐Home period of the study, yielding an adherence rate of 99%.

results.finding: HemoCare distiller output reportedly met ISO 23500-3 for hemodialysis water. Sample size and measured values were unreported.
results.detail: The comparison text cites ISO 23500-3, while the product-water row lists ISO 23000-3. The FDA letter records a substantial-equivalence decision, and the compliance statement comes from the submitter’s summary.

results.finding: In a home peritoneal dialysis study (22 enrolled, 14 completed), 56.9% of tap-water purification samples were reported as passing ISO 13959. The sample count was unspecified.
results.detail: The authors attribute the reported water-purity pass rate to missing laboratory data. The abstract reports no separate counts for measured failures and missing results.
results.quote: Missing data for water purity attributed to only 56.9% of samples passing.

results.finding: The modified 2008K@home hemodialysis machine with bibag met predefined test acceptance criteria. Sample size and numerical results were unreported.
results.detail: Home use requires observation by a trained, qualified person. The filing identifies an optional blood and water leak detector but gives no home-specific hazard analysis findings.
results.quote:
Test results demonstrated that the modified 2008K@home Hemodialysis Machine with
bibag System functions as intended and met pre-determined acceptance criteria.

results.finding: The modified Fresenius Liberty Cycler met functional acceptance criteria in testing that included a 6-liter dialysate bag (sample size unreported).
results.detail: The submission reports passing IEC 62366 usability testing. It does not describe the home-use scenarios tested or identify the home-specific hazards addressed by the risk analysis.
results.quote:
Test results demonstrated that all modifications functioned as intended and met pre-
determined acceptance criteria.

results.finding: FDA cleared the Byonyks X-1 APD Cycler and DS-1 under K243371. The applicant’s summary specifies home use. No clinical studies were conducted.
results.detail: The applicant’s Indications for Use section lists acute and chronic peritoneal dialysis. Its separate Environment of Use section names the home setting.
results.quote:
The Byonyks X-1 APD Cyler is prescribed for use in both professional healthcare Facility and 
Home Environment.

definition = "A system that can travel with the patient would remove waste and excess fluid through an external blood filter (hemodialysis) or the lining of the abdomen (peritoneal dialysis). It would cost less than US$1,000 to manufacture at scale and less than US$5 a day to run, operate on solar power, purify water from any source and match the safety and effectiveness of existing dialysis. In a home pilot of the prize-winning design, patients prepared peritoneal dialysis fluid from tap water. The pilot tested the fluid without using it for treatment.". Reason: The definition now explains what portability permits and how far the closest prototype progressed.

goal.need = "In 2010, at least 2.284 million people may have died prematurely because they could not get dialysis or a kidney transplant. For someone using four 2-litre bags a day for peritoneal dialysis, about three tonnes of fluid must be delivered each year. A cheaper machine leaves that freight bill in place. Preparing fluid locally could reduce the cost of home treatment. Solar power and local water could also bring dialysis within reach of remote communities, where patients still need access to clinical care.". Reason: The access estimate gains a concrete explanation of the recurring cost patients face and the clinical support they would still need.

add statement by International Society of Nephrology, Asian Pacific Society of Nephrology and The George Institute for Global Health, Affordable Dialysis Prize, 2015: "It needed to cost less than US$1000 to build at scale and provide treatment for less than $5 a day". Reason: The statements omit the prize sponsors who set the entry’s manufacturing and daily treatment cost targets.

add not found: "No statement from a nephrology society or prize body disputing the value or feasibility of the combined targets was located.". Reason: The available prize and society statements address the goal’s rationale without disputing its value or feasibility.

edit completion: threshold_quote = "It needed to cost less than US$1000 to build at scale and provide treatment for less than $5 a day, be able to run on solar power, using any water source, yet be as safe and effective as existing dialysis systems."; threshold_ref = 4; basis = "The prize sponsors set design targets and awarded the prize in March 2016 while the prototype was in development. In the subsequent home pilot, three patients filled 60 peritoneal dialysis bags using potable Sydney tap water in homes with reliable electricity. Two bags had detectable endotoxin. No participant received dialysis with the prepared fluid. Comparative clinical performance and operation under the full prize conditions remain unverified."; refs = [4, 5, 6, 16]. Reason: The full prize sentence supports all four parts of the test, and the home pilot identifies exactly what the winning prototype demonstrated.

add milestone after None: "A purifier produces water that meets the quality limits for preparing the intended dialysis fluid.". Reason: Water purification can be tested before a complete dialysis prototype is available, and the required output quality depends on how the water will be used.

edit m1: criterion = "Functional testing verifies that the prototype performs as designed. A system-level hazard analysis and evidence of electrical safety and electromagnetic compatibility address the intended environment, including hazards specific to home use when that use is claimed."; threshold_quote = "functional testing that demonstrates that the device performs as designed and expected;"; threshold_ref = 7. Reason: The bench criterion currently includes two clearance histories alongside the functional and safety tests.

edit m2: criterion = "An early human feasibility study documents delivery of dialysis with the investigational system and assesses device function and initial clinical safety."; threshold_quote = "Early feasibility studies allow for early clinical evaluation of devices to provide proof of principle and initial clinical safety data."; threshold_ref = 10. Reason: The feasibility criterion mixes the test with enrollment counts, adverse events and publication status from individual studies.

edit m3: criterion = "After training, patients or care partners deliver prescribed dialysis at home. For nocturnal home hemodialysis, compare adverse events, delivery of the prescribed dose and completion of scheduled treatments with in-clinic use. For wearable peritoneal dialysis, the AWAK protocol trains patients for independent use, sets an individual prescription and measures the proportion of treatments completed over seven days at home. Its study defined completion as delivering at least 70% of the prescribed sorbent dialysis in a treatment."; set_by = "FDA nocturnal home hemodialysis guidance, section 5, for the clinic comparison. AWAK Technologies protocol NCT05827588 for the seven-day peritoneal dialysis assessment, with the per-treatment endpoint specified in the Kidney Week abstract."; set_by_kind = "protocol"; threshold_quote = "use the AWAK PD system at home for at least 7 days"; threshold_ref = 30; refs = [15, 30, 31, 8, 16]. Reason: The registered AWAK study supplies a home-treatment test for peritoneal dialysis, where the existing criterion cites only a fluid-preparation pilot.

edit m4: criterion = "FDA issues a 510(k) decision letter finding the dialysis system substantially equivalent to a legally marketed device, and the indications for use accompanying the decision explicitly include home treatment."; threshold_quote = "This order \u201cclears\u201d the device for commercial distribution"; threshold_ref = 17. Reason: The clearance test depends on FDA’s decision and the enclosed indications, while the names and dates of cleared devices belong with the results.
